stories.headline: Lessons from Nepal’s Flood Catastrophe
stories.title: Lessons from Nepal’s Flood Catastrophe
stories.summary: The images emerging from Nepal are terrifying, but they are also instructive. Entire settlements washed away, roads cut off, lives lost, and hundreds still missing — the scale of the tragedy is a grim reminder that the Himalayas are no longer a distant postcard of beauty, but a living zone of danger. For Kashmir, the lesson is not merely emotional sympathy. It is urgent self-examination. What is unfolding in Nepal should force us to look closely at our own vulnerabilities. Kashmir, too, sits in a seismic, fragile, and flood-prone Himalayan belt. Our rivers swell quickly, our slopes remain unstable, our drainage systems are overburdened, and our unplanned urban expansion continues to ignore the basic logic of geography. Every time disaster strikes elsewhere, we express concern. But concern without preparedness is only a temporary emotion. The first lesson from Nepal is that nature does not wait for governance to catch up. By the time warnings are fully understood, the damage is already done. This is especially true for mountain regions where cloudbursts, landslides, flash floods, and glacial lake outbursts can turn a few hours of rain into a catastrophe. Kashmir has witnessed enough such events to know that “this cannot happen here” is the most dangerous sentence in public life. The second lesson is the cost of weak infrastructure. Roads, bridges, embankments, drainage channels, and hillside settlements must be planned for extreme events, not average weather. A river does not negotiate with concrete. A slope does not respect political promises. If construction continues to outrun safety planning, then every development project carries within it the seed of future destruction. The third lesson is social preparedness. Communities that know evacuation routes, emergency contact points, and safe shelters survive better than those left to improvisation. Schools, panchayats, local bodies, and disaster management agencies must build a culture of drills and awareness. Relief cannot begin only after the water enters homes. It must begin long before the clouds gather. There is also a deeper moral lesson. Climate change is no longer an abstract debate for seminars and policy papers. It is now lived reality in the mountains. The Himalayas are warming, weather patterns are becoming erratic, and the old assumptions about seasons and safety are collapsing. To treat such disasters as isolated events is to miss the larger warning. Nepal’s flood tragedy should therefore become a wake-up call for Kashmir’s planners, administrators, and citizens alike. We need stronger embankments, smarter land-use policies, better weather forecasting, stricter regulation of construction, and far more serious investment in disaster readiness. Most of all, we need humility before the landscape we inhabit. The mountains are speaking. The question is whether we are listening.

stories.headline: 'Our parents were crossing the border an hour before the flood hit'
stories.title: 'Our parents were crossing the border an hour before the flood hit'
stories.summary: Authorities say nearly 2,000 people are missing, including more than 100 Americans and Canadians, as families await word on loved ones after the Nepal flash floods.
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: Hundreds of foreign nationals are desperately waiting to hear from loved ones thought to be caught in the deadly flash flood and mudslide along the Nepal-Tibet border.
Sisters Shreya and Ashna Ahuja are among those anxiously waiting for some news of their parents, Deepak and Madhu Ahuja, who had travelled from Texas to Mount Kailash on a group pilgrimage.
"It's only been one day, but it has felt like much longer," the sisters tell the BBC.
"We just love them a lot and want them to come home." One of the siblings spoke to their parents just before the floods struck.
Nearly 2,000 people are missing, including tourists from the US, Australia, Canada, India, and the UK.
Nepali authorities say more than 575 people have died.
About 90 US citizens may have been impacted by the floods, the State Department said on Thursday, confirming that five Americans in Nepal have made their way to safety.
The Ahuja sisters have contacted the State Department and US embassies in Delhi, Nepal and China, but they say they have no concrete information on the whereabouts of their parents.
The region is a pilgrimage site for Hindus and Buddhists, and visited by tens of thousands of pilgrims each year.
Radhika Sharma's parents, Ramesh Sharma, 65 and Neelam Sharma, 64, two US citizens who live in New York City, were also travelling to Mount Kailash in the Kathmandu region when the disaster struck.
The pilgrimage was their first trip on their own since retiring last year.
"I am just trying to find them, I don't have any answers," Radhika Sharma told the BBC.

stories.headline: Resignation will come, accountability first: Ruhullah writes to NC Chief
stories.title: Resignation will come, accountability first: Ruhullah writes to NC Chief
stories.summary: Srinagar, Aug 28: Srinagar MP and National Conference leader Aga Syed Ruhullah Mehdi has escalated his differences with party president Dr Farooq Abdullah, saying he would resign but insisting that “accountability must come first”. In a detailed letter to Abdullah dated August 28, Ruhullah questioned the National Conference’s position on the restoration of Article 370 and argued that statehood cannot be treated as a substitute for the constitutional protections removed in August 2019. Ruhullah said he was responding to recent remarks by Abdullah, including, “How long will you be a slave? You have to stand on your feet sometimes. When will you stand?” He also referred to Abdullah’s reported remark, “You want 370, but you beg from Delhi.” Addressing Abdullah as “Doctor Sahab”, Ruhullah said the remarks reflected a frustration felt by many people in Jammu and Kashmir. “I must confess, those words resonated deeply with me. They captured a frustration many of us in Jammu-Kashmir feel: that even while asking for what is rightfully ours, we are expected to assume a posture of supplication before the BJP,” he wrote. Ruhullah questioned the party’s current emphasis on restoration of statehood instead of Article 370 and 35A. He said statehood was a right recognised by the Supreme Court and had also been promised by the BJP in its 2024 Assembly election manifesto. Accepting statehood as the limit of the party’s demands, he argued, would amount to “legitimising and normalising the constitutional assault of August 2019”. Ruhullah also questioned why the NC included restoration of Articles 370 and 35A in its 2024 election manifesto if the party believed the commitments could not be fulfilled. “Were we making promises we knew we could not keep or perhaps never truly intended to keep?” he asked. He said he did not want to be part of what he described as a political “lie”, alleging that he had faced a “coordinated campaign of rebuke” within the party over his position. Defending his position, Ruhullah said Article 370 represented the struggle for the dignity, constitutional guarantees and liberties of the people of Jammu and Kashmir. He also highlighted unemployment, land and resources, religious rights, language, traditions and environmental degradation as issues requiring political attention. “Nearly 65% of Jammu and Kashmir's population is young, and their future is increasingly uncertain, with no jobs and opportunities. Our land is up for grabs. Our resources benefit everybody but us,” he wrote. He said elected representatives should seek stronger constitutional safeguards rather than limit their aspirations to what the BJP government was willing to concede. Ruhullah also referred to Abdullah’s political record, recalling that he was chief minister when the erstwhile Jammu and Kashmir Assembly passed the Autonomy Resolution. “I do not ask these questions out of disrespect. I ask them because I remember that you were the Chief Minister of the very Assembly that passed the Autonomy Resolution. That, too, must have required courage,” he wrote. “What has changed, the aspirations of our people, or the JKNC's willingness to stand up for them?” he asked. On the question of his resignation, Ruhullah said he would await Abdullah’s response to the issues raised in his letter. “There are many more questions. But for now, I will await your response to these and so will the people of Jammu-Kashmir, who have a right to know what the JKNC truly stands for,” he wrote. “Rest assured, the resignation will come. It would have come even without you asking but before that must come accountability.” The letter marks a further escalation in Ruhullah’s differences with the NC leadership over Article 370, statehood and the party’s political position on the constitutional changes of August 2019.
